messages.content:
Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "the survey export for the eastbank neighborhood is being assembled from paper forms and the online form, and the current folder has one spreadsheet for each collection week. the first week covers april 3 through april 9, while the next file covers april 10 through april 16. a few paper forms came in after the first week had been entered, so those answers are in a separate tab marked late paper. they still belong with the first week, but they should stay in that tab until the coordinator checks the entry dates. the online responses already carry a submission date, although a blank date appears on two records where the connection dropped during submission. those two records are listed on the review sheet and should not be assigned a date from the paper forms.

1. the folder also includes the question list, the short introduction shown to participants, and a copy of the map used to define the eastbank boundary. in the question list, question 6 asks how often someone uses the riverside path, and its answer choices are daily, weekly, monthly, and never. a note beside the question says that people could choose one answer, not several. the export has a column for each response, and the empty cells in those columns mean no answer was recorded. they do not mean that the person selected never. this distinction matters because the summary sheet counts answers by choice, and a blank cell should remain blank unless a response is present in the source form. the coordinator's working copy has a separate comments column for questions that were difficult to read.

on the first tab, the neighborhood names appear in the order they were used on the paper forms, with Eastbank listed before Mill Landing and North Quay. the online form offered those same names in a drop-down menu, but two participants typed a street name instead. the export leaves those entries as typed and marks them for review; it does not replace them with a neighborhood based on the street. the boundary map is there to help with checking the wording, not to make an automatic assignment. if a street name is unclear, the reviewer can add a note in the comments column and leave the neighborhood response as it is. there is also one response that says “near the old ferry stop,” which is the participant's wording and is copied from the paper form.

The spreadsheet has a date column and a source column on each weekly tab. the source column says paper or online, except for the late-paper tab where it also records the date the form was entered. that entry date is not the date the person completed the survey. on the paper forms, participants were asked to write the completion date near the top, but several left it empty. the blank dates remain blank in the export, and no date should be inferred from the collection week. a paper form collected on april 8 might have been filled in earlier, and the export does not establish when that happened. the weekly tabs are for organizing the records, not for filling missing dates. the two online records with no submission date should stay flagged on the review sheet until the coordinator can inspect the available form details.

There are a few spelling differences between the paper and online versions of the question about bus access. the paper sheet asks whether a participant can reach a bus stop within ten minutes on foot, while the online version says within a 10-minute walk. both versions refer to the same question, and the export stores their answers in the same column. the original wording is kept in the question list so that anyone reviewing the export can see which version appeared on the form. a participant wrote “not sure, maybe if the hill is dry” in the comments box. that phrase is copied as written, and it is not converted into yes or no. the form provides no separate answer option for that kind of comment, so the response remains in the comments field beside the participant's other answers.

For the file handling, do not rename files. the existing file names include the week dates and the source type, and the coordinator uses those names when matching a tab to the paper bundle. an allowed action is to sort a working copy by submission date, while leaving the original tabs in their current order. the dates with no value will appear together at the end of that sort, but they should still be treated as missing, not as a date range or as a late submission. if someone makes a working copy, the copy should retain the source column and the review flags, because those fields show why certain records have not been grouped with the others. the original export remains available alongside any working copy.

The paper bundles are kept in two envelopes, one for forms collected at the library table and one for forms collected at the riverside booth. the location is written on the envelope, not on every form, so the export does not have a collection-location value for each participant. the coordinator's notes say that the library table was staffed on april 5 and april 12, while the riverside booth was open on april 6 and april 13. those dates describe the collection schedule, not the completion date of an individual form. a form in the library envelope may have been filled out before it was handed in. the location notes are stored in the folder beside the export and are not additional survey answers.

The summary sheet is still a working sheet and contains totals by question, but it does not include names or contact details. the survey form did not ask participants for their names, and the export has no name column. each record has an internal row number added for checking entries across the tabs. that row number is not a participant number printed on the form, and it should not be read as an order of participation. one paper response was entered twice while the coordinator was comparing the handwriting with the spreadsheet; the two entries are marked as a possible duplicate, not removed. the source form is still in its envelope, and the review sheet points to both row numbers so they can be compared.

The coordinator also has a small note about the map version: the boundary line along Dock Street was updated before the survey started, while the copy in the folder shows the earlier line. the question list refers to the named neighborhoods, not to a boundary decision, and the map copy has not been used to change any responses. the folder records which map was included with the original materials so that the discrepancy can be seen during review. Separately, the next collection week begins on april 17, and its spreadsheet has been created with the same columns as the earlier tabs. the first paper bundle for that week has not yet been entered, and the file currently contains its headings only. The online form remains open through april 23, as stated in the participant introduction.", "output": "The Eastbank neighborhood survey export is being assembled from paper forms and the online form. They do not mean that the participant selected “never.” This distinction matters because the summary sheet counts answers by choice. A blank cell should remain blank unless a response appears on the source form. The coordinator’s working copy has a separate comments column for questions that were difficult to read.

The online form offered the same names in a drop-down menu, but two participants typed a street name instead. The export leaves those entries as typed and marks them for review; it does not replace them with a neighborhood based on the street. The boundary map is there to help check the wording, not to make an automatic assignment. If a street name is unclear, the reviewer can add a note in the comments column and leave the neighborhood response as it is. One response says “near the old ferry stop.” This is the participant’s wording, copied from the paper form.

Each weekly tab has a date column and a source column. The source column says “paper” or “online,” except on the late-paper tab, where it also records the date the form was entered. That entry date is not the date the person completed the survey. Participants were asked to write the completion date near the top of the paper forms, but several left it blank. Blank dates remain blank in the export, and no date should be inferred from the collection week. A paper form collected on April 8 might have been filled in earlier, and the export does not establish when that happened. The weekly tabs organize the records; they are not a reason to fill in missing dates. The two online records with no submission date should remain flagged on the review sheet until the coordinator can inspect the available form details.

There are some spelling differences between the paper and online versions of the question about bus access. The paper sheet asks whether a participant can reach a bus stop within ten minutes on foot, while the online version says “within a 10-minute walk.” Both versions refer to the same question, and the export stores their answers in the same column. The original wording remains in the question list so that anyone reviewing the export can see which version appeared on each form. One participant wrote, “not sure, maybe if the hill is dry,” in the comments box. That phrase is copied as written and is not converted into yes or no. The form has no separate answer option for that kind of comment, so the response remains in the comments field beside the participant’s other answers.

For file handling, do not rename files. The existing file names include the week dates and source type, and the coordinator uses them to match a tab to the paper bundle. One allowed action is to sort a working copy by submission date while leaving the original tabs in their current order. Dates with no value will appear together at the end of that sort, but they should still be treated as missing, not as a date range or a late submission. If someone makes a working copy, it should retain the source column and review flags because those fields show why certain records have not been grouped with the others. The original export remains available alongside any working copy.

The paper bundles are kept in two envelopes: one for forms collected at the library table and one for forms collected at the riverside booth. The location is written on the envelope, not on each form, so the export does not have a collection-location value for every participant. The coordinator’s notes say that the library table was staffed on April 5 and April 12, while the riverside booth was open on April 6 and April 13. Those dates describe the collection schedule, not the completion date of an individual form. A form in the library envelope may have been filled out before it was handed in. The location notes are stored in the folder beside the export and are not additional survey answers.

The summary sheet is still a working sheet. It contains totals by question but does not include names or contact details. The survey form did not ask participants for their names, and the export has no name column. Each record has an internal row number added to help check entries across the tabs. That row number is not a participant number printed on the form, and it should not be read as the order of participation. One paper response was entered twice while the coordinator was comparing the handwriting with the spreadsheet. The two entries are marked as a possible duplicate, not removed. The source form is still in its envelope, and the review sheet points to both row numbers so they can be compared.

The coordinator also has a short note about the map version: the boundary line along Dock Street was updated before the survey started, while the copy in the folder shows the earlier line. The question list refers to named neighborhoods, not to a boundary decision, and the map copy has not been used to change any responses. The folder records which map was included with the original materials so that the discrepancy can be seen during review. Separately, the next collection week begins on April 17, and its spreadsheet has been created with the same columns as the earlier tabs. The first paper bundle for that week has not yet been entered, and the file currently contains headings only. The online form remains open through April 23, as stated in the participant introduction."}]
